There also exist policy- driven markets, such as the market for low-carbon fuel standard (LCFS) credits in California42. EV operators accrue LCFS credits for displacing petroleum consumption with less-carbon- intensive electricity, which they can sell on the LCFS market. A ChaaS provider can facilitate participating in the LCFS market and realize LCFS-derived incomes. Finally, the presence of EVSE can also serve as a marketing tool to draw customers, for example, to shop at a grocery store while their EVs charge. Each of these revenue generation opportunities requires special expertise that a ChaaS provider might offer. Technical functions The challenge of designing an EV charging system is best categorized as a technical challenge that requires expert knowledge and experience achieve optimal outcomes. Even for a system as simple as residential EVSE, customers may not be familiar with the implications of fundamental design decisions, such as power capacity and location, with respect to factors such as existing electricity infrastructure and building codes. This can lead to the risk of mis-specifying the system, which can increase costs and/or diminish performance. The potential for suboptimal design decisions only increases as system complexity increases, not only because the knowledge required for design increases but also because the opportunity to optimize for cost improves. EVSE system design support documents compiled for consumers, residents of multi-unit dwellings (MUDs), businesses, and fleets, many of which are not representative of current best practices, span dozens of pages and cover topics ranging from the basics of energy and power measurement units to the different types and costs of trenching. While these purport to facilitate the design and installation process, they also serve to highlight the unavoidable complexity faced when designing an EV charging system. More innovative technical additions to a system, such as automated charging management (smart charging) or the integration of DERs, can drastically reduce operating costs and improve performance (as we demonstrate in Section 4.4), but substantially increase the design complexity. For all of these reasons, the technical design and operations expertise of a ChaaS provider can offer value to customers. Managerial functions The managerial functions served by ChaaS can be divided into categories of system interfacing and product life cycle management. System interfacing functions address the interface between the customer and entities from other systems, including the electricity provider and regulating authorities. When installing and operating EV charging, a typical user is expected to choose between pricing models, identify applicable incentive programs, work with the utility to implement connection upgrades, and respond to price signals, among other responsibilities43. They are also responsible for following all pertinent regulations, which are often not straightforwardly communicated. None of these are commonsense tasks, even if utilities and regulating authorities devote substantial resources to clear communication, and customers unfamiliar with how to perform these tasks risk overpaying to use underperforming systems, or even facing penalties for breaking regulations.
